Milky Way's fastest star

Astronomers have discovered the fastest known star in our galaxy, the Milky Way, orbiting the black hole at its centre. The star, named S301, was detected with the European Southern Observatory's Very Large Telescope Interferometer in Chile's Atacama Desert, after more than two decades of careful observation by several teams of researchers.

At its closest approach the star races past the black hole at a large fraction of the speed of light, making it the fastest star ever measured in the Milky Way. Tracking a single faint star so close to the galactic centre required combining the light of four separate telescopes into one sharp virtual instrument, a technique that took years to perfect.

The result offers a new way to test how gravity behaves in the most extreme environment in our galaxy, close to a black hole four million times the mass of the Sun. The measurements line up with the predictions of general relativity, even under conditions far harsher than anything that can be reproduced on Earth.

Future instruments are expected to sharpen the measurement further and reveal still more stars on similar orbits. The team hopes that the next generation of telescopes, now under construction, will let them watch the star complete a full loop around the black hole and probe the nature of gravity in even finer detail.

More information

This research was presented in a paper to appear in Astronomy & Astrophysics.
